extra.message: Missing authentication on sensitive routes — Any anonymous attacker can upload files, execute OS commands, read arbitrary server files, and extract database credentials without any credentials. [verified: No authentication decorators, session cookies, or access-control checks exist on any handler; the login form at /login.html authenticates but sets no session, leaving upload, command execution, and file read fully exposed to anonymous users.]

SQL Injection in login handler — Authentication bypass, extraction of all user credentials (plaintext passwords), database manipulation or deletion. [verified: Username and password from POST body (lines 102-103) are interpolated via string concatenation into a raw SQL query at lines 106-107 without parameterized queries or any escaping — enables authentication bypass and full database extraction.]

OS Command Injection via server ping tool — Remote code execution on the host OS as the user running the Tornado process — full server compromise. [verified: User-controlled 'server' POST parameter (line 124) is concatenated directly into os.popen('ping -c 3 ' + server) at line 125 with zero sanitization, escaping, or allowlisting — trivial command injection via ;, |, or && chaining.]

Path traversal — arbitrary file read via StaticHandler — Disclosure of arbitrary files on the server filesystem accessible to the process, including credentials, source code, and system files. [verified: URL path captured by r'/static/(.*)' is prepended with 'static/' then os.path.join'd at lines 40-42; '../' sequences resolve through os.path.join, allowing escape from the static/ directory to read arbitrary files like test.db or /etc/passwd.]

Path traversal — arbitrary file read via ContentHandler — Disclosure of the SQLite database (plaintext credentials), application source code, and potentially any file readable by the process on the server filesystem. [verified: The 'file' query parameter (line 75) is concatenated directly into io.open('read/' + file_name) at line 77 with no os.path.basename or '..' rejection — attacker can read test.db, server.py, or /etc/passwd via ../ sequences.]

Cross-Site Request Forgery on all POST endpoints — One-click command execution or file upload via a victim's browser session; enables CSRF-to-RCE when combined with the command injection in ServerHandler. [verified: No xsrf_cookies setting, no _xsrf hidden fields in templates, and no CSRF checks on any of the three state-changing POST handlers (login, server ping, upload); an attacker can craft a cross-origin form to achieve CSRF-to-RCE via the /server.html command injection.]

Plaintext Passwords Exposed in Application Logs — User plaintext passwords captured in application logs are accessible to administrators, log aggregation systems, and anyone who gains access to log files or stdout output [verified: UsersHandler.post at server.py:99 prints self.request.body to stdout, which contains the raw POST body with plaintext username and password from every login attempt, with no redaction or suppression.]

Passwords stored in plaintext — If the database is compromised (trivial via SQL injection or path traversal), all user passwords are immediately usable, enabling credential-stuffing attacks and full account takeover. [verified: create_db() at lines 140-148 inserts passwords as plaintext into the TEXT column with no hashing or salting; combined with SQL injection and path traversal, all credentials are trivially extractable and immediately usable.]

Debug mode enabled in application configuration — Information disclosure — stack traces reveal source code paths, variable contents (potentially including credentials or tokens), and internal application logic to unauthenticated attackers. [verified: Tornado Application settings at line 31 unconditionally set 'debug': True with no environment check, exposing full stack traces, local variables, and source snippets to unauthenticated users on any unhandled exception.]

Unrestricted file upload with preserved extension — Upload of malicious files (web shells, scripts, HTML with embedded JS) that persist on disk and can be accessed or executed through secondary attack vectors. [verified: POST /upload accepts any file preserving the client-supplied extension and writes to /tmp/ with no content-type validation, auth, or signature checking; uploaded HTML can be served with text/html Content-Type via the StaticHandler path traversal (finding 3) for stored XSS.]

Denial of Service via Unbounded File Upload Size — Attacker exhausts server disk space by uploading large files, causing denial of service for all application functionality including database operations and log writes [verified: UploadHandler.post at server.py:66 writes file1['body'] to /tmp/ with no application-level size validation; Tornado's default max_body_size (~100MB) provides a framework-level bound but allows repeated multi-MB uploads that can exhaust disk space.]

Browser XSS Auditor Explicitly Disabled — Removes browser XSS filter protection, making the reflected XSS in the search endpoint trivially exploitable in browsers that would otherwise block the attack [verified: SearchHandler at server.py:88 explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection: 0; the search template (templates/search.html) uses {% raw query %} and {% raw link %}, creating a genuine reflected XSS sink that the disabled browser XSS auditor would otherwise mitigate in supporting browsers.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint — Unrestricted brute-force attacks against user credentials, enabling credential guessing and account takeover with no detection or throttling. [verified: No rate-limiting, progressive delay, account lockout, or CAPTCHA exists on the login POST handler at line 98 — enabling unrestricted automated brute-force against the plaintext-stored credentials.]

Log Injection (CRLF) via Unsanitized Request URI and Body — Attacker injects forged log lines to cover tracks, frame other users, corrupt log-based monitoring/alerting, and poison log analysis pipelines [verified: Six print statements across server.py (lines 53,86,95,99,120,126) output unsanitized self.request.uri and self.request.body, allowing CRLF (%0d%0a) injection to forge log entries, obscure attack traces, or corrupt log analysis.]

Weak PRNG used for uploaded file name generation — Predictable upload filenames allow an attacker to guess or overwrite files uploaded by other users, or to access files before the legitimate user does. [verified: random.choice (Mersenne Twister, non-cryptographic) is used for upload filename generation at line 63 instead of secrets or os.urandom; theoretical filename predictability exists but practical impact is minimal since files land in /tmp/ and are already trivially reachable via path traversal.]
